slides.title: Bunyan Building Permits Authority must choose a configuration of Watad
slides.text: The case study Bunyan Building Permits Authority must choose a configuration of Watad Watad answers applicants' questions on building regulations, in Arabic and English. Four configurations are candidates: Plain prompt Regulation retrieved Small open-weight model A B Mid-size open-weight model C D The logs 600 questions from 80 regulation documents, five samples per question at temperatures 0.2 and 0.8, a model grader's verdict on every answer. Synthetic, fixed seed.

slides.title: An evaluation is a sample
slides.text: Session 1 An evaluation is a sample Explain what population an evaluation score estimates Compute the formula standard error of a pass rate Bootstrap a pass rate and compare the two intervals 01

slides.title: An evaluation is an experiment, and its questions are a sample
slides.text: The frame An evaluation is an experiment, and its questions are a sample Population every question applicants could ask about the regulations → Sample the 600 questions someone wrote → Estimate D passes 74.7% of them The question a reader cares about is how D would do on questions not yet written. The 74.7% is an estimate of that, with a standard error.

slides.title: A pass rate is a mean of zeros and ones, so it has a standard error
slides.text: The formula A pass rate is a mean of zeros and ones, so it has a standard error ±1.8 points: the standard error of D's first sample, 600 questions SE = √(p(1 − p) / n) with p = 0.747 and n = 600 gives 0.0178. A 95% interval is p ± 1.96 SE: 71.2% to 78.1%. Four times the questions halves the standard error. AI-off. Work this first standard error by hand, with a calculator, before Lab 1.1 asks for it in code.

slides.title: Resample the questions to see how much the score would move
slides.text: The bootstrap Resample the questions to see how much the score would move 1 · Draw 600 questions with replacement → 2 · Score the pass rate of the draw → 3 · Repeat 5,000 times → 4 · Read the spread is the standard error No formula needed: the same recipe works for medians, differences and corrected rates later in the course.

slides.title: With 600 independent questions, the formula and the bootstrap agree
slides.text: Lab 1.1 result With 600 independent questions, the formula and the bootstrap agree Method SE 95% interval Formula 0.0178 71.2% to 78.1% Bootstrap over questions, 5,000 draws 0.0178 71.2% to 78.2% Bootstrap over documents 0.0254 wider: session 2

slides.title: The interval is about new questions, not about these 600
slides.text: Reading an interval The interval is about new questions, not about these 600 It says If questions were written again the same way, intervals built like this would contain D's true pass rate 95% of the time. It does not say That D passes between 71.2% and 78.1% of these 600 questions: on these, the rate is known exactly. And it is silent on questions of a different kind: dialect, new regulations, other agencies.

slides.title: A score travels with its interval, its n, its samples and its temperature
slides.text: Reporting A score travels with its interval, its n, its samples and its temperature D: 74.7% (95% CI 71.2 to 78.1), 600 questions, 1 sample each, temperature 0.2 Without the interval, a one-point lead looks like a win. Without n, samples and temperature, nobody can reproduce or compare it.

slides.title: What does the interval describe?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does the interval describe? Configuration B scores 69.8% on the 600 questions, 95% interval 66.7% to 72.9%. A manager asks what the interval means. Which answer is right? B passes between 66.7% and 72.9% of these 600 questions B's pass rate on questions written the same way is plausibly between 66.7% and 72.9% Each answer of B passes with a probability between 66.7% and 72.9% B will score between 66.7% and 72.9% on next year's regulations

slides.title: A pass rate with two intervals
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min A pass rate with two intervals Bootstrap configuration D's pass rate on the 600 questions and compare the interval with the one from the formula standard error. D1_1_bootstrap_pass_rate.ipynb Load the logs and compute the pass rate of one sample 4 min The formula standard error and a 95% interval 5 min A bootstrap over questions 8 min Compare the two intervals and the two distributions 5 min Write the score as a reader should see it 3 min ✱ Stretch: Bootstrap over documents and say why the interval widens

slides.title: Clustered items
slides.text: Session 2 Clustered items Explain why items from one source document are not independent Compute a standard error clustered by document Report the design effect and the effective number of items 02

slides.title: Questions written from one document succeed and fail together
slides.text: How the items were written Questions written from one document succeed and fail together Khattab's team wrote 4 to 9 questions from each of 80 regulation documents. A document the model reads well yields many passes; an obscure one, many failures. So the 600 questions are not 600 independent draws: they are 80 clusters. What it does Formulas that assume independence understate the standard error. The interval is too narrow and differences look more certain than they are.

slides.title: Sum the deviations inside each document before squaring
slides.text: The clustered standard error Sum the deviations inside each document before squaring def clustered_se(x, groups): x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float) sums = pd.Series(x - x.mean()).groupby(groups).sum() return np.sqrt((sums ** 2).sum()) / len(x) Deviations of the same sign inside one document add up, so a document whose questions fail together contributes much more than nine independent questions would.

slides.title: The design effect says how many independent questions the 600 are worth
slides.text: Design effect The design effect says how many independent questions the 600 are worth DEFF = (SE clustered / SE naive)² Effective number of questions: n / DEFF D: naive SE 0.0151, clustered 0.0234 2.4 D's design effect: 600 questions are worth about 249 independent ones

slides.title: Every configuration's interval widens by half once documents are counted
slides.text: Lab 1.2 result Every configuration's interval widens by half once documents are counted Config Mean Naive SE Clustered SE DEFF Effective n A 63.2% 0.0165 0.0281 2.88 209 B 69.8% 0.0156 0.0258 2.72 221 C 72.1% 0.0153 0.0244 2.54 236 D 74.3% 0.0151 0.0234 2.41 249

slides.title: Resample documents, or ask statsmodels for cluster covariance
slides.text: Two checks Resample documents, or ask statsmodels for cluster covariance Cluster bootstrap Draw 80 documents with replacement and keep all their questions: SE 0.0231 against 0.0234 by formula. statsmodels OLS on a constant with cov_type="cluster": 0.0236, the formula times √(G / (G − 1)). Few clusters. With 8 categories as clusters the estimate is itself noisy; with 80 documents it is stable.

slides.title: New documents buy more precision than more questions per document
slides.text: What it means for writing items New documents buy more precision than more questions per document 120 more questions from the same 80 documents The document effects stay; the clustered SE barely moves. 120 questions from 16 new documents More clusters: the clustered SE falls by about the square root of 96/80.

slides.title: Which change narrows the interval most?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which change narrows the interval most? C's design effect is 2.5. Furat can pay for 160 more questions. Which plan narrows C's clustered interval most? 160 questions from the same 80 documents, two per document Ten samples per question in place of five 160 questions from 20 new documents Report the naive interval, which is already narrower

slides.title: Clustered by document
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min Clustered by document Compute standard errors clustered by source document for four configurations, the design effect and the effective number of items, and check the formula with a cluster bootstrap and statsmodels. D1_2_compute_standard_errors.ipynb Questions per document and pass rate per document 4 min The clustered standard error by formula 7 min Design effect and effective number of items 5 min A cluster bootstrap as a check 5 min statsmodels with cluster covariance as a second check 4 min ✱ Stretch: Cluster by category instead and explain why eight clusters are too few

slides.title: Repeated samples
slides.text: Session 3 Repeated samples Split the variance of a score into item and sampling parts Predict the standard error for K samples per item Distinguish the mean pass rate, pass@k and pass^k 03

slides.title: A score varies because of which questions were written and because the model samples
slides.text: Two sources of noise A score varies because of which questions were written and because the model samples Between items Some questions are easy, some hard. Only more questions reduce this part. Within items Asked twice, the model may answer differently. More samples per question reduce this part. Var(question mean) = between + within / K for the mean of K samples per question.

slides.title: At temperature 0.8 the model's own randomness is more than half the variance
slides.text: Lab 1.3 result At temperature 0.8 the model's own randomness is more than half the variance 0.2 · between 0.123 0.2 · within 0.068 0.8 · between 0.087 0.8 · within 0.124

slides.title: Five samples help; twenty barely help more
slides.text: What more samples buy Five samples help; twenty barely help more Samples per question SE at 0.2 SE at 0.8 1 0.0179 0.0187 5 0.0151 0.0136 20 0.0145 0.0124 600 questions, configuration D, ignoring clustering. The floor is the between-item part.

slides.title: The mean, pass@5 and pass^5 answer three different questions
slides.text: Pass rates over repeated attempts The mean, pass@5 and pass^5 answer three different questions Estimand The question it answers D at 0.2 D at 0.8 Mean per sample One answer to one applicant 74.3% 70.0% pass@5 Right at least once in five tries 86.7% 91.2% pass^5 Right every time in five 59.2% 41.2%

slides.title: Fix the temperature and the samples in the plan, not after the results
slides.text: Temperature is part of the design Fix the temperature and the samples in the plan, not after the results Evaluate at the temperature the deployed configuration will use. At temperature 0, sampling variance is near zero, but the score still has between-item error. Report the samples per question and how they were combined.

slides.title: Twenty samples per question
slides.text: Checkpoint Twenty samples per question At temperature 0.2, D's between-item variance is 0.123 and its within-item variance 0.068. A colleague proposes 20 samples per question in place of 5 to "make the score precise". What happens? The standard error barely falls, because the between-item part does not shrink with samples The standard error halves, as it would with four times the questions The pass rate rises, because more samples find more right answers The score becomes pass@20, which is the right metric at last

slides.title: Item and sampling variance
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Item and sampling variance Split the variance of the pass rate into item and sampling parts at temperatures 0.2 and 0.8, and predict how the standard error falls with more samples per question. D1_3_split_variance_into.ipynb One row per question: the mean of five samples 4 min Within-item variance at each temperature 6 min Between-item variance, corrected for sampling 6 min The standard error for 1, 5 and 20 samples 5 min pass@5 and pass^5 next to the mean 4 min ✱ Stretch: Check the predicted standard error for K = 2 by subsampling the logs

slides.title: Plan before results
slides.text: Session 4 Plan before results Explain how choices made after the results inflate false wins Write an analysis plan for a comparison of two configurations State a minimum effect and a decision rule in advance 04

slides.title: Each choice made after seeing the results is another chance of a false win
slides.text: Choices after the results Each choice made after seeing the results is another chance of a false win Metric mean, first sample, pass@5 Subset all, Arabic, one category Analysis paired or not, clustered or not Exclusions drop "broken" questions Every path is defensible alone. Choosing the one that wins is what inflates the error rate.

slides.title: Choosing the best of four metrics after the fact triples the false wins
slides.text: Lab 1.4 result Choosing the best of four metrics after the fact triples the false wins One planned metric 5.2% Best of four, chosen after 16.3% 2,000 simulated comparisons of two identical configurations, 600 questions, five samples each.

slides.title: The plan fixes the question, the metric, the analysis and the decision
slides.text: What a plan fixes The plan fixes the question, the metric, the analysis and the decision Field For C against D Question Is D at least three points better than C? Primary metric mean grader pass rate per sample, 5 samples, temperature 0.2 Analysis paired difference D minus C, clustered by document Minimum effect 3 points; alpha 0.05; power 0.8 Slices language and category, declared now

slides.title: A difference can be real and still too small to act on
slides.text: The minimum effect A difference can be real and still too small to act on Switching configurations costs migration, retesting and serving. Dr. Nadeen will switch only for three points or more. Written before the results, the threshold cannot drift to fit them. Three verdicts Worth switching; real but too small to matter; not shown. The plan says which interval leads to which.

slides.title: Write what each possible interval leads to, before you see it
slides.text: The decision rule Write what each possible interval leads to, before you see it Whole interval above 3 points switch to D ↓ Above 0, but includes values below 3 D is better; whether by enough is not shown ↓ Includes 0 no difference shown; keep C

slides.title: Commit the plan to git before the results exist
slides.text: Evidence that the plan came first Commit the plan to git before the results exist git add plan.json git commit -m "Commit the analysis plan" # later, in a separate commit git add results/ analysis/ The commit history is the timestamp the capstone review checks. An amendment is a new dated commit with its reason, never a silent edit.

slides.title: The metric changed after the results
slides.text: Checkpoint The metric changed after the results The plan named the mean pass rate. After the run, D beats C on pass@5 but not on the mean. The team wants to headline pass@5 "because it shows D's potential". What should the report do? Headline pass@5, since it is a recognised metric Headline pass@5 with alpha lowered to 0.01 Delete pass@5 from the report entirely Headline the planned mean and label pass@5 as an unplanned, exploratory result

slides.title: A plan before the results
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min A plan before the results Draft a pre-registered plan comparing configurations C and D, validate it against the required fields, and simulate how choosing among four metrics after the results inflates false wins. slides.title: Comparing systems
slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Statistical Evaluation of AI Systems Comparing systems Day 2: Decide whether one configuration beats another, and plan an evaluation big enough to tell Data Science Track4 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-403

slides.title: Comparing systems
slides.text: Today Comparing systems Session 1 · Paired designs The same questions for both configurations: the paired difference, its standard error, and a verdict against a minimum effect Session 2 · Many configurations Six configurations and fifteen comparisons: family-wise error, adjusted intervals and ranks that are honest about ties Session 3 · Sizing an evaluation How many questions are needed to detect a three-point difference: the power formula with a design effect, checked by simulation Session 4 · Spending the budget More questions or more samples per question at a fixed cost, with the grader calls in the budget

slides.title: Which standard error belongs in the report?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which standard error belongs in the report? A new task set has 400 questions from 40 documents. The naive standard error of a configuration's score is 0.020 and the clustered one is 0.032. Which should the report use, and what does it imply? The naive one: it is more precise The mean of the two, 0.026 Either, if each question was sampled five times The clustered one: the 400 questions are worth about 156 independent ones

slides.title: Paired designs
slides.text: Session 1 Paired designs Compute a paired difference with a clustered standard error Explain the width of paired and unpaired intervals from the correlation Write a verdict against a minimum effect 01

slides.title: C and D answered the same 600 questions, so compare them question by question
slides.text: The design you already have C and D answered the same 600 questions, so compare them question by question Unpaired Two scores, two standard errors, combined as if the question sets were different. Paired One difference per question, D minus C, and the standard error of that one column. Same mean, different width. Both estimate D minus C = 2.2 points; only the paired analysis uses the fact that the questions are shared.

slides.title: Hard questions are hard for both, and the difference removes what they share
slides.text: Why pairing helps Hard questions are hard for both, and the difference removes what they share Var(D − C) = Var(D) + Var(C) − 2 Cov(C, D) Unpaired analysis drops the covariance term. With a strong positive correlation it overstates the variance of the difference several times over. 0.83 correlation of C's and D's per-question scores

slides.title: Pairing makes the interval four times narrower than the clustered unpaired one
slides.text: Lab 2.1 result Pairing makes the interval four times narrower than the clustered unpaired one Analysis of D minus C SE 95% half-width Unpaired, naive 0.0215 ±4.2 points Unpaired, clustered 0.0338 ±6.6 points Paired, naive 0.0089 ±1.7 points Paired, clustered by document 0.0086 ±1.7 points

slides.title: One column of differences, one clustered standard error
slides.text: The calculation One column of differences, one clustered standard error t = U.paired_table("C", "D", 0.2) # one row per question d = t["diff"].mean() # 0.0217 se = U.clustered_se(t["diff"], t.doc_id) # 0.0086 lo, hi = d - 1.96 * se, d + 1.96 * se # 0.005 to 0.039

slides.title: D is better than C, but not shown to be better by three points
slides.text: The verdict against the minimum effect D is better than C, but not shown to be better by three points 0 3 points: minimum effect 2.2 (0.5 to 3.9) Paired, clustered by document; 600 questions, five samples at temperature 0.2 (Lab 2.1).

slides.title: Three lines the decision owner can act on
slides.text: The decision note Three lines the decision owner can act on Paired difference D minus C: 2.2 points, 95% CI 0.5 to 3.9, clustered by document, 600 questions, 5 samples, temperature 0.2. Minimum effect: 3 points. Verdict: better, not shown to matter. The unpaired analysis would have given ±6.6 points and no conclusion. At temperature 0.8 the difference is 2.9 points, CI 0.8 to 5.0: the same verdict.

slides.title: Two configurations on the same questions
slides.text: Checkpoint Two configurations on the same questions Two configurations answer the same 500 questions. Their scores' intervals overlap heavily. A colleague concludes there is no difference. What is wrong with that? Overlapping separate intervals ignore the correlation; the paired interval of the difference can exclude zero The intervals should have been clustered first Nothing: overlapping intervals mean no difference The difference must be checked against the minimum effect before anything else

slides.title: Many configurations
slides.text: Session 2 Many configurations Explain why fifteen comparisons need adjustment Compute Bonferroni and Holm adjusted paired intervals Report a ranking with the set of plausible ranks 02

slides.title: Six configurations mean fifteen comparisons, and fifteen chances of a false separation
slides.text: Many configurations Six configurations mean fifteen comparisons, and fifteen chances of a false separation F · D, Arabic system prompt 76.5% D · mid-size, retrieval 74.7% E · D, long instructions 74.7% C · mid-size, plain 73.2% B · small, retrieval 70.0% A · small, plain 62.7% One greedy sample per question, 600 questions, temperature 0.2. The naive ranking crowns F.

slides.title: Adjust the threshold to the number of comparisons you make
slides.text: Family-wise error Adjust the threshold to the number of comparisons you make Method Rule Pairs separated Unadjusted each test at 5% 10 Bonferroni each test at 5% / 15; intervals with z = 2.94 6 Holm k-th smallest p against 5% / (15 − k + 1), stop at the first failure 8 Both adjustments keep the chance of any false separation among the fifteen at 5%. Holm never separates fewer pairs than Bonferroni.

slides.title: Sizing an evaluation
slides.text: Session 3 Sizing an evaluation Derive the number of items from the paired variance, the design effect and the minimum effect Check a sizing formula by simulation over documents Explain what the pilot can and cannot tell 03

slides.title: Size the evaluation for the difference that matters, not for the one you hope to see
slides.text: Before the next evaluation Size the evaluation for the difference that matters, not for the one you hope to see The effect Three points, from Dr. Nadeen: the minimum worth a switch. The errors 5% false alarm, 80% power: a true three-point gain is found four times in five. The noise The spread of per-question differences, from a pilot.

slides.title: Questions needed grow with the square of the noise over the effect
slides.text: The formula Questions needed grow with the square of the noise over the effect n = (z0.975 + z0.80)² × s² / δ² = (1.96 + 0.84)² × 0.219² / 0.03² 0.219 SD of the per-question difference D minus C 0.93 design effect of the difference: floored at 1 417 questions, about 56 documents

slides.title: Sizing a single score with the naive formula falls far short
slides.text: Where the design effect bites Sizing a single score with the naive formula falls far short Paired difference DEFF about 1: the documents cancel. 417 questions. Unpaired, each score DEFF about 2.4 5,826 questions per configuration for the same three points. The same rule for a single score: to estimate D's pass rate within ±2 points, multiply the naive n by its design effect of 2.4.

slides.title: Resample documents from the pilot, plant three points, run the planned test
slides.text: Check by simulation Resample documents from the pilot, plant three points, run the planned test 1 · Draw 56 documents with replacement → 2 · Plant shift differences to a mean of 3 points → 3 · Test clustered paired interval above 0? → 4 · Count 2,000 times

slides.title: At the formula's 417 questions the simulated power is 85%
slides.text: Lab 2.3 result At the formula's 417 questions the simulated power is 85% 300 questions 71% 417 questions 85% 900 questions 99% The formula is slightly conservative here, because the difference's design effect is below 1 and the formula floored it.

slides.title: Three lines that go into the committed plan
slides.text: The sizing plan Three lines that go into the committed plan Detect D minus C = 3 points (paired, two-sided, alpha 0.05) with 80% power: 417 questions from about 56 documents, 5 samples each at temperature 0.2. Pilot: 600 questions of the 2026 set; SD of the per-question difference 0.219; design effect 0.93; simulated power at 417 questions 85%.

The decision needs to detect 3 points. Which inputs should the sizing use? The 6-point difference and SD 0.25 The 3-point minimum effect and SD 0.25 3 points and the SD of each configuration's scores 200 questions, since the pilot already found a difference

slides.title: Spending the budget
slides.text: Session 4 Spending the budget Write the variance of a score as a function of items and samples Find the number of samples per item that minimises variance at fixed cost Include grader calls and human labels in an evaluation budget 04

slides.title: Every riyal buys either new questions or more samples of the old ones
slides.text: A fixed budget Every riyal buys either new questions or more samples of the old ones Unit (synthetic costs from Furat) SAR A new question, written and reviewed in both languages 15.00 One sample: a generation 0.04 One sample: a grader call 0.06 A human label of a grader verdict 4.00 Budget of the next evaluation 6,000

slides.title: The variance falls with questions and samples; the cost rises with both
slides.text: The trade-off The variance falls with questions and samples; the cost rises with both Variance (between + within / K) / n Cost n × (15 + 0.10 K) ≤ 6,000 Minimising the first under the second gives K* = √((15 / 0.10) × within / between).

slides.title: The optimum is flat: from five to ten samples changes the error by 1%
slides.text: Lab 2.4 result The optimum is flat: from five to ten samples changes the error by 1% Temperature K* Best design SE At K = 5 0.2 9.1 375 questions × 10 0.0186 387 × 5: 0.0188 0.8 14.7 368 questions × 13 0.0162 387 × 5: 0.0170 Questions cost 150 samples each, so several samples per question pay; more of them pay at 0.8, where sampling noise is larger.

slides.title: Leave the grader out of the cost and you over-sample; leave people out and you cannot correct
slides.text: What the budget must include Leave the grader out of the cost and you over-sample; leave people out and you cannot correct Grader call forgotten K* at 0.2 rises from 9.1 to 14.4: the plan buys samples it cannot afford to grade. Human labels reserved SAR 1,200 for 300 labels leaves 300 questions × 10: SE 0.0208 instead of 0.0186.

slides.title: With documents in the picture, new questions should come from new documents
slides.text: One more term With documents in the picture, new questions should come from new documents The between-item part is inflated by the design effect, about 2.4 for one score. That favours spending on questions over samples, and on documents over questions per document. A full model has three costs: a document, a question, a sample.

slides.title: Spending the next SAR 6,000
slides.text: Checkpoint Spending the next SAR 6,000 A new question costs SAR 15 and a sample with its grader call SAR 0.10. At temperature 0.8 within-item variance exceeds between-item variance. Which design is closest to the best at a fixed budget? As many questions as possible, one sample each Few questions, thirty samples each Whatever K, since the grader cost does not enter About ten to fifteen samples per question, the rest on questions

slides.title: A 95% interval should contain the true rate in 95% of evaluations
slides.text: Coverage A 95% interval should contain the true rate in 95% of evaluations 1 · Fix a true rate p and a size n → 2 · Draw thousands of evaluations → 3 · Build an interval for each → 4 · Count how many contain p Only n + 1 outcomes are possible, so the coverage can also be computed exactly by summing binomial probabilities.

slides.title: Wald is the formula of Day 1; three others behave better near the edges
slides.text: Four intervals for a proportion Wald is the formula of Day 1; three others behave better near the edges Interval Idea 38 of 40 Wald p ± 1.96 √(p(1 − p) / n) 0.883 to 1.018 Wilson inverts the score test; centre pulled toward 0.5 0.835 to 0.986 Clopper-Pearson exact, from Beta quantiles; never under-covers 0.831 to 0.994 Jeffreys Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior, posterior interval 0.849 to 0.989

slides.title: With 20 items at 98%, Wald covers the truth one time in three
slides.text: Lab 3.1 result With 20 items at 98%, Wald covers the truth one time in three Coverage at p = 0.98 n = 20 40 80 200 Wald 0.32 0.55 0.81 0.90 Wilson 0.94 0.96 0.98 0.93 Jeffreys 0.94 0.96 0.98 0.96 Clopper-Pearson 0.99 0.99 0.98 0.96

slides.title: Near 1, Wald's estimated variance collapses exactly where it is least reliable
slides.text: Why Near 1, Wald's estimated variance collapses exactly where it is least reliable At 40 of 40, √(p(1 − p) / n) = 0: the interval is the single point 1. At 39 of 40 it is narrow and centred too high. The rate's distribution is skewed near the edge; Wald assumes symmetry. 87% Wald's exact coverage at n = 40, p = 0.95

slides.title: Small or extreme: Wilson or Jeffreys; a safety claim: Clopper-Pearson
slides.text: A rule for the standard Small or extreme: Wilson or Jeffreys; a safety claim: Clopper-Pearson Hundreds of items, rate mid-range Any interval; the clustered one for documents. Fewer items, or within 0.1 of an edge Wilson or Jeffreys: near 95% on average. A claim that must not under-cover Clopper-Pearson: at least 95%, wider.

slides.text: Checkpoint Choosing an interval for a small set A new circular yields 25 questions; configuration D passes 24. The report needs a 95% interval for D's pass rate. Which choice is sound? p ± 1.96 √(p(1 − p) / n), the standard formula A bootstrap over the 25 questions A Wilson or Jeffreys interval, or Clopper-Pearson if it supports a safety claim No interval: 25 items are too few to say anything

slides.title: Forty questions where a wrong answer could hurt someone
slides.text: Bunyan's safety set Forty questions where a wrong answer could hurt someone A 36 / 40 B 38 / 40 C 39 / 40 D 40 / 40 One greedy answer per question per configuration; each marked safe or unsafe by Sereen's panel. Topics: exits blocked during works, load-bearing walls, fuel in basements, floors added without a structural report, steep ramps.

slides.title: Forty out of forty does not mean never
slides.text: The edge case Forty out of forty does not mean never [1, 1] Wald: certainty from 40 questions 0.928 one-sided 95% lower bound, 0.051/40 7.2% the unsafe rate the data cannot rule out The rule of three gives nearly the same: 3 / 40 = 7.5%.

slides.title: Clopper-Pearson comes from two Beta quantiles
slides.text: Exact intervals Clopper-Pearson comes from two Beta quantiles def clopper_pearson(k, n, level=0.95): a = 1 - level lo = 0.0 if k == 0 else stats.beta.ppf(a / 2, k, n - k + 1) hi = 1.0 if k == n else stats.beta.ppf(1 - a / 2, k + 1, n - k) return lo, hi D, 40 of 40: 0.912 to 1. C, 39 of 40: 0.868 to 0.999. A, 36 of 40: 0.763 to 0.972.

slides.title: A Beta prior and k of n give a Beta posterior, and its interval
slides.text: Bayesian intervals A Beta prior and k of n give a Beta posterior, and its interval prior Beta(a, b) → posterior Beta(a + k, b + n − k) Uniform prior, Beta(1, 1): D 0.914 to 0.999. Jeffreys prior, Beta(0.5, 0.5): D 0.940 to 1.000. State the prior At 40 of 40 the prior moves the lower end by 2.6 points. In a safety claim the uniform prior is the more cautious of the two.

slides.title: Is C safer than A? Probably, but 40 questions cannot settle it
slides.text: Comparing on a small set Is C safer than A? Probably, but 40 questions cannot settle it 0.90 posterior probability that C's safe rate exceeds A's (39/40 against 36/40) Draw from both uniform posteriors, count how often C is ahead. A one-in-ten chance that A is in fact at least as safe. For a release gate, set the threshold before looking.

slides.title: Write what the 40 questions show, and stop there
slides.text: The release note Write what the 40 questions show, and stop there Safety set (40 questions, one greedy answer each): D was safe on 40 of 40; with 95% confidence its unsafe-answer rate on such questions is below 7.2% (one-sided Clopper-Pearson). C 39/40, B 38/40, A 36/40.

slides.text: Session 4 Correcting for grader error Correct an observed pass rate with sensitivity and specificity Carry calibration uncertainty into the interval by bootstrap Report corrected and uncorrected rates by language 04

slides.title: Solve the grader's mixing for the true pass rate
slides.text: The correction Solve the grader's mixing for the true pass rate observed = θ × sens + (1 − θ) × (1 − spec) θ = (observed + spec − 1) / (sens + spec − 1) Example C in Arabic: observed 0.692, sens 0.921, spec 0.735, corrected 0.652. It needs sens + spec above 1, and it leaves 0 to 1 when the observed rate is below 1 − spec or above sens.

slides.title: The correction lowers Arabic rates four times as much as English ones for C
slides.text: Lab 3.4 result The correction lowers Arabic rates four times as much as English ones for C Observed Corrected Change C, Arabic 69.2% 65.2% −4.1 C, English 75.0% 74.1% −0.9 D, Arabic 74.2% 72.7% −1.5 D, English 74.3% 73.4% −1.0

slides.title: The corrected rate is uncertain because of the test set and because of the calibration set
slides.text: Two sources of uncertainty The corrected rate is uncertain because of the test set and because of the calibration set Test set only Clustered SE of the observed rate divided by (sens + spec − 1): ±8.3 points for C in Arabic. Too narrow. Both Resample documents of the test set and, independently, the calibration verdicts; recompute sens, spec and the correction each time.

slides.title: Resample both sets, then correct
slides.text: One replicate Resample both sets, then correct pick = rng.integers(0, len(sums), size=len(sums)) # documents p = sums[pick].sum() / cnts[pick].sum() j = rng.integers(0, len(h), size=len(h)) # calibration verdicts sens = v[j][h[j] == 1].mean() spec = 1 - v[j][h[j] == 0].mean() draw = (p + spec - 1) / (sens + spec - 1)

slides.title: The correction holds only if the grader errs on test answers as it did on calibration answers
slides.text: The assumption The correction holds only if the grader errs on test answers as it did on calibration answers Calibrate per language, and per configuration if their answers differ in style. Draw calibration answers from the same population as the test answers. Re-calibrate when the grader, its prompt or the configurations change.

What is wrong? Nothing: the correction removes the grader's error The interval ignores the uncertainty of sensitivity and specificity, so it is too narrow The calibration set should have been clustered by document too Corrected rates should be reported without intervals

slides.title: A validator turns the standard into a gate
slides.text: Make it checkable A validator turns the standard into a gate def validate(report): problems = [f"missing: {f}" for f in STANDARD if not report.get(f)] if not {"ar", "en"} <= set(report.get("slices") or {}): problems.append("slices: Arabic and English required") if report.get("shared_items") and "paired" not in report.get("comparison", ""): problems.append("comparison must be paired") return problems

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How presentations are scored The rubric Plan 20% Uncertainty and comparison 25% Sizing 15% Grader correction and slicing 20% Reporting and reproducibility 20% Two or more open-weight configurations, each measured. A claim without an interval is a plan, not a result.

slides.title: Fifteen minutes each: ten to present, five for the challenge
slides.text: Format Fifteen minutes each: ten to present, five for the challenge 1 · The plan The claim, the minimum effect, the clustering unit; the plan.json commit and its date. 2 · The results Scores with clustered intervals, the paired verdict, Arabic and English after the grader correction. 3 · One choice One statistical choice you made, and what the other choice would have cost. Peer feedback. After each review, everyone writes one strength, one question and one suggestion.

slides.title: The assessor changes one choice; you predict the consequence before re-running
slides.text: Inside the fifteen minutes The assessor changes one choice; you predict the consequence before re-running Change drop a cluster of documents, or raise the minimum effect → Prediction which interval moves, whether the verdict changes, and why → Re-run analyze.py on the changed input, on screen What earns the marks. A prediction with a reason, then an honest reading of the re-run, whichever way it went.

slides.title: The supervised check: three tasks on paper
slides.text: First, AI-off · 30 minutes · 20% The supervised check: three tasks on paper A clustered standard error From a short table of per-document sums, by hand, with the design effect it implies. Paired or unpaired Two designs described in words: choose the analysis and say which interval is narrower. Read a sizing plan Are the questions enough for the stated minimum effect, and what is missing. Calculators allowed; laptops and phones closed. At least 60% here is needed to pass.
